To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we have developed a system that automatically classifies punctate protein patterns into distinct subclasses, (2) we have used this system to annotate hundreds of new punctate proteins, and (3) we have built generative models that capture the key features of each subclass.

(i) we developed an automated approach to the classification of punctate protein distribution patterns, and (ii) we developed a generative approach for modeling the spatial distribution of punctate protein distributions in relation to microtubule distributions.

the problem of automated characterization and classification of punctate protein distributions.
automated analysis and classification of punctate protein localization, and we have developed a system that can be applied to the analysis of large numbers of proteins.
the problem of automated analysis of protein distributions from images.

the system described here provides automated analysis of the spatial distribution of punctate proteins, including quantification and characterization of their relationship to microtubule networks, and can be used for large-scale annotation of subcellular localization of proteins in microscopy images.
this work provides a new and powerful approach for the analysis of protein patterns in microscopy images that can be applied to a wide variety of proteins and cell types.

the proposed approach can be used to automatically annotate the spatial distributions of proteins in microscopy images, and that the resulting patterns can be modeled in a manner that provides a basis for simulation of cellular behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the spatial distribution of punctate proteins is much more complex and varied than has previously been recognized, that these patterns are highly reproducible across cell types and experimental conditions, and that these patterns can be automatically characterized and quantified.
we were able to show how a large-scale microscopy image database can provide new information about protein localization, which in turn can lead to a better understanding of cell biology.

we have demonstrated that it is possible to automatically analyze the spatial distributions of proteins directly from confocal microscopy images and that the resulting information is of high value for understanding protein localization and for constructing models of cell behaviors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the patterns of punctate proteins are highly diverse, and that they can be characterized with automated methods.
automated analysis of microscopy images can be used to provide a more comprehensive and quantitative description of subcellular protein distributions than is possible by visual inspection.

automated image analysis can be used to identify patterns of subcellular localization that are not obvious to human observers, and that the resulting models can be used for further biological discovery.
